PHBR3 p.123. The holy book of a faith, written in the distant past either by the god or by a believer obeying his word. It records important events from the faith's history, explains the requirements the god makes of his followers, and explains his philosophy, goals and concerns. NOT A MAGICAL WORK, and it does NOT act as a holy symbol -- it cannot be used to confront vampires or similar monsters. COST DERIVED, NOT INVENTED: the book calls a canon 'a mere 200 sheets (400 pages)' and prices it at 400 gp in paper alone at 2 gp per sheet, plus 50 gp for binding. That matches this file's own Paper, Sheet at 2 gp (PHB), so the figure is internally consistent with data already held. A priest should have saved enough to commission one SOMETIME BETWEEN 3RD AND 5TH LEVEL; one who reaches 6th without acquiring a copy is viewed with suspicion by commoners and fellow priests alike, who will question his devotion. He carries it wherever he travels and should make every effort to recover a stolen one. Not all faiths have an individual written canon: some share a common one, some transmit it orally, some have none at all. WEIGHT IS AN ESTIMATE, not printed -- the book gives no figure; 5 lb is a 400-page bound volume and should be replaced if a printed weight ever surfaces.

PHBR3 p.123 PRINTS THIS PRICE AND EXPLAINS IT, which is why an otherwise unattributed row now has a source. In a temple of the god, THREE priests of 2nd level or higher stand over an empty water-basin and pray for the god's blessing for a full hour, then cast simultaneously: one create water, the second protection from evil, the third purify food & drink. That makes HALF A GALLON. create water alone can make up to four gallons, but the other two spells each cover only half a gallon, so every additional PAIR of priests casting those two adds another half-gallon -- NINE priests together reach the four-gallon ceiling. The expenditure of magic and the hour of time are the reason a single dose costs 25 gp to an adventurer; any three priests of 2nd level or higher of the same god can make it 'for free'.

PHBR1 p.117. A mechanical device rather than merely a sheath, worn on the arm just below the elbow. BUILT FOR EXACTLY ONE OF: dagger, knife, or stiletto -- a sheath for one WILL NOT HOLD either of the other two, and cannot be built for any weapon outside those three. Record which weapon this sheath is built for, and which of the character's weapons sits in it, in the notes field on the card. Straightening the arm and flexing it pops the blade into the hand. The character must make a DEXTERITY ABILITY CHECK to catch it, with a +3 BONUS, but A NATURAL 20 ALWAYS FAILS. On a failure the blade pops straight out and drops to the floor; it CANNOT be 'shot out' as an attack, will not hurt whomever it hits, and always lands hilt-first when fumbled this way. IN COMBAT the character must announce BEFORE INITIATIVE IS ROLLED that he intends to pop the blade. When his action comes up, if he is still able to straighten his arm, the blade pops into his hand and is instantly ready -- and HE MAY STILL ATTACK that round, since arming himself does not use up an attack. Non-magical. The cost and weight here are the SHEATH ALONE; the weapon it holds is recorded separately. MANUFACTURE requires someone with BOTH the Set Snares AND Weaponsmithing proficiencies. Used by rogues, street-fighters, assassins, and characters wishing to appear unarmed. LEGALITY (PHBR1 p.117): Illegal in most places, but a lesser crime than the spring-out spike: punishable by a fine of 10d6 gp and a few days (1d6) in jail.

PHBR2 p.91. A plain cloth sling worn to make the thief appear to have a broken or injured arm; he withdraws the hand from it for the attempt. REDUCES PICK POCKETS BY 5%, but HALVES the chance of being discovered -- a natural 00 on d100 still always means discovery. People do not expect a man with a broken arm to be picking pockets and the expectation determines the perception. Worth using when the priority is not being caught rather than succeeding: a thief working a city where he is not a guild member, or where the penalties are harsh. Cannot be used for an extended period in the same place -- there is a limit to how long an arm can plausibly need healing.

PHBR2 p.91. A generic term for a very small, usually very sharp blade held between the fingers or in the edge of the hand. A sharpened coin edge, filed down, serves and is readily available. Used to CUT a soft container -- a purse or pouch -- so the thief can reach what is inside; the most effective technique for getting at coins and gems inside a purse with drawn and tied strings. WITH a mini-blade the thief makes ONE pick pockets roll. WITHOUT one he must open the purse strings and then extract the contents: TWO pick pockets rolls, and TWO rolls for being observed. Not a weapon -- the book gives it no damage and describes no combat use.

PHBR2 p.91. A more sophisticated and rarer form of the mini-blade: a hollow signet ring with a flip-top and a very sharp blade within. Same purse-cutting function and the same one-roll-instead-of-two effect on pick pockets. Not a weapon.

PHBR2 p.91. As the iron razor ring, in silver -- a hollow signet ring with a flip-top concealing a very sharp blade, used to cut purses and pouches. The book prices the two separately but gives them one description; the silver version is the one that passes as jewellery. Not a weapon.

PHBR2 pp.91-92. For a lock the thief's best efforts cannot pick. The lock must make a SAVING THROW FOR METAL VS. ACID (save 13). If the save succeeds the lock cannot be opened; it is then RUINED AND UNOPENABLE if a second metal-vs-acid save is failed. Takes 3d6 rounds. Only acids of great strength work -- black dragon acid, thessalhydra acid, possibly giant slug spittle -- which is why availability is very low and cost very high, and why the DM should greatly restrict it. Thieves avoid it: the glass or ceramic vessel is fragile (imagine falling down a pit and hearing it break), a failed job may destroy any other hope of opening the lock, and it is a calumny on a professional's reputation to need it.

PHBR2 p.92. Used with a small hammer to FORCE a lock rather than pick it. BASE CHANCE EQUALS THE CHARACTER'S OPEN DOORS PERCENTAGE (Strength-based), and a thief may ADD ONE-FIFTH OF HIS OPEN LOCKS CHANCE to that base -- knowing something about locks helps a little. Not really a highly skilled activity, so the DM might extend it to non-thieves. Takes one turn. Noisy: any hope of subtlety and surprise evaporates with the first blow.

PHBR2 p.92. A hacksaw or equivalent, for sawing through a lock apparatus or cutting around a lock when picking has failed and the thief has time. Usually only reasonably small locks can be cut through. Fairly noisy, though nowhere near as noisy as a lock chisel. The main drawback is time: cutting AROUND a lock takes 2d6 turns (wooden door of average thickness), cutting THROUGH a lock 3d6 turns. In most cases the attempt is certain to succeed barring special circumstances.
PHBR2 p.92. A spare or bare blade, usable on its own to saw through a lock or to cut around one. Same slow-but-near-certain outcome as the full hacksaw.

PHBR2 p.92. Used like a hacksaw blade to saw through a lock apparatus. Slow and fairly noisy, but usually certain to work in the end -- unless the circumstances are against it, e.g. one small rusty file against a huge combination lock.
PHBR2 p.92. A pair of small wire cutters, useful for disabling part of a lock's internal mechanism when the lock cannot be picked.

PHBR2 pp.92-93. A long-necked funnel, sometimes with a short length of rubber tubing on the end, for applying light oil to the inside of a rusted or dirty lock. The DM may apply penalties (-5, -10, etc.) to open locks for such a lock -- dungeon door locks are all too often of this sort -- and LUBRICATION NEGATES THAT PENALTY IN WHOLE OR IN PART. Takes 1 round to apply and 1d6+4 rounds to take effect. Oil also helps the thief work silently: IF THE DM CALLS FOR A MOVE SILENTLY CHECK FOR LOCK-PICKING, IT IS MADE AT +10 WHEN OIL IS USED. Also useful on rusty door hinges.

PHBR2 p.93. Padded footwear -- the item a whole type of robber is named after. Can be improvised from rags or cloth tied to the feet, or built into footwear, the latter removing any risk of the cloth falling off. ADDS +5 TO MOVE SILENTLY. THE CORRESPONDING DISADVANTAGE IS -5 TO ANY CLIMB WALLS ROLL, because footpads reduce traction -- which is why they are NOT considered standard equipment worn by a thief. The normal move silently chance assumes ordinary footwear; the DM may apply a penalty for hob-nailed boots or the like.

PHBR2 p.93. Lengths of stiff, hardened leather, usually 30 to 36 inches long, laid down ahead of the thief to spread his weight over a wider area. THEIR USE NEGATES ANY NEGATIVE MODIFIER ARISING FROM SQUEAKY FLOORBOARDS -- and nothing else; they do not improve move silently in general. The thief must pick the strips up and move them before him as he walks, HALVING the move silently movement rate, i.e. one-sixth of normal walking movement.

PHBR2 p.94. Black or very deep blue clothes, usually voluminous robes or a 'utility suit', lightweight enough to be carried easily and worn under normal clothing. ALWAYS INCLUDES SIGNIFICANT FACIAL COVERING. ADDS +5% TO HIDE IN SHADOWS in any area that is shadowy, or at a light level equal to dusk or early dawn or equivalent. Meant to be used with charcoal on the face, neck and backs of the hands for a further +2%. Exceptional variants exist for specific settings -- crimson clothing to hide among the crimson curtains of a lady's boudoir, for instance.

PHBR2 p.94. Similar in basic design to a darksuit but made of light clothing dyed in irregular patterns of greens and browns. ADDS +5% TO HIDE IN SHADOWS when the thief conceals himself in a suitable OUTDOOR setting -- woodland, a field, the garden of a town house. The outdoor counterpart of the darksuit, and pairs with plant dye the way the darksuit pairs with charcoal.

PHBR2 p.94. Crushed leaves, berries, certain oily barks and the like, used to disguise the exposed face and hands. ADDS A FURTHER +2% TO HIDE IN SHADOWS in suitable OUTDOOR settings -- the outdoor analogue of charcoal, and meant to be used with a woodland suit. Such plant materials are usually rather sticky and smelly.

PHBR2 p.94. A thick, oil-based emulsion coated onto any metal surface, rendering it almost completely matte black and reflection-free, against the glint of a steel weapon in moonlight or torchlight. THE BOOK OFFERS TWO RULES AND PREFERS THE SECOND: (a) if the DM wishes, +5 to hide in shadows; (b) THE SUPERIOR RULE -- its use SAVES THE THIEF A SECOND HIDE IN SHADOWS ROLL if he draws a weapon while hiding, or saves him from any penalty modifier if a weapon is already drawn when he first attempts to hide. Once the weapon has struck a blow the weaponblack is wiped off. BEING OIL-BASED IT IS HIGHLY FLAMMABLE: if ignited it burns brightly, turning the weapon into the equivalent of a flame tongue (though NOT a magical weapon) for 1d4+1 rounds, but an unprotected wielder takes 1d4 damage per round while holding it.

PHBR2 p.94. A cone of bronze, brass or similar, the wide end placed against the surface the thief wishes to hear through and the narrow end against his ear. ADDS +5 TO DETECT NOISE. A generous DM may allow one improvised from a wine glass. WISE TO FIT MESH OVER THE BROAD END to exclude ear seekers -- the chapter's opening story turns on exactly that. A miniaturised version may be needed to listen for the tumblers of a combination lock; see the combination-lock rule under Open Locks, where a successful detect noise roll HALVES the negative modifier.

PHBR2 p.95. Three or four hooks branching from a central point, attached to a rope. CLIMBING A WALL USING A GRAPPLING HOOK AND ROPE ADDS +40% TO THE NORMAL CLIMB WALLS CHANCE. Landing success is rolled on Table 29 by target type. NOISE: a successful landing can be heard up to 400 yards away in near silence, an unsuccessful throw (the clang as it hits the ground) up to 800 yards; PADDING the iron with sacking or similar heavy coarse cloth over almost all its surface HALVES that range. A DM may rule that shards of glass set into the top of a wall sever a grappling line in 2d6 rounds. NOT THE SAME RECORD AS THE PHB'S GRAPPLING HOOK (8 sp, 4 lb), which is a different and heavier item; both are kept.

PHBR2 p.97. To be effective these must be used together with a line. Hammering one in takes 1d4 rounds with a small hammer. THEY WILL NOT TAKE IN VERY SMOOTH SURFACES -- with the exception of an ICE WALL, where spikes are the only hope of climbing safely. Hammering can usually be heard a long way off, up to a mile in silent, windless outdoor conditions. Usually used as insurance against falls: a character who hammers in a spike, ropes himself to it and climbs 20 feet above it falls only 40 feet (20 down to the spike, 20 more taking up the slack). A SPIKE ARRESTING A FALL HAS A 10% CHANCE PER CHARACTER SUPPORTED ON THE LINE OF COMING LOOSE, 15% per character for ice wall ascension. NO-STACKING: p.90 names climbing daggers and spikes as its own example of two items that do the same thing, so their climb walls modifiers may not be added together.
PHBR2 p.97. Used with tar paper, which is affixed to the centre of the area of glass to be cut so the pane can simply be pulled away once the cutter has done its work.

PHBR2 p.97. A harness of straps carrying small metal rings to which many devices can be affixed -- tools hung, climbing daggers fixed, and suchlike. TWO PRINCIPAL USES: (i) climbing a rope, the thief clips one or more rings of the harness to the rope, removing any chance of falling from letting go; (ii) working at height, two of the straps are fixed either side of him (usually with climbing daggers, or wedges in a window frame) to give a firm base and FREE BOTH HANDS to open a lock, cut glass, check for traps and the like. This is the climbing dagger's main intended use, per p.95.

PHBR2 pp.97-98. Molds, files, small blades and metal-working instruments, plus a small oil-burning apparatus for softening and molding metal -- so its use is normally restricted to a safe lair. Duplicating a key takes 1d4 hours. Produces poor- to fair-quality soft-metal replicas, rough in appearance and clearly not professional work. THE DUPLICATE OPENS THE SAME LOCKS AS THE ORIGINAL IF THE THIEF MAKES A SUCCESSFUL DEXTERITY TEST, WHICH THE DM SHOULD ROLL IN SECRET. If the duplicate was made from a WAX PAD IMPRESSION rather than the key itself there is a PENALTY OF +2 to that roll. The thief always believes his work is a success; only trying the lock reveals otherwise. A SKELETON KEY CANNOT BE DUPLICATED with a keymaking set. Does not pre-empt locksmiths, who duplicate keys at 99% with individually crafted tools too complex for a thief who is not himself a locksmith.

PHBR2 p.98. Strips of very thin, very tough resilient wood, around 4 to 6 inches long and an inch high, often coated one or both sides with a thin toughening varnish. Slipped between a door and its frame so the thief can raise a latch on the far side and open the door normally, possibly after picking a lock. A NORMAL LATCH CAN BE OPENED; A BAR IS TOO STRONG FOR A LIMEWOOD STRIP TO LIFT. Other similar woods serve.

PHBR2 p.98. Thick cloth sewn with hundreds of tiny curved barbed hooks, all lying the same way, so it feels smooth stroked in one direction and grips -- even tearing skin or cloth -- in the other. Affixed to a surface with the hooks pointing DOWNWARD it holds tools and other items in place: they are simply pressed onto it and stick. Most useful to a thief climbing a wall. SHARKSKIN-COATED GLOVES CAN BE USED TO ASSIST CLIMBING WALLS AND ARE TREATED AS CLAWED GLOVES IN ALL RESPECTS -- see the Clawed Gloves weapon record for the surface-by-surface table and the move silently penalty.

PHBR2 pp.98-99. Deliberately held back from the Open Locks section because the DM will almost certainly want to restrict these drastically, if they exist at all. FOUR SUGGESTED TREATMENTS, the DM's pick: (1) BY QUALITY -- keys come in good, excellent or superior (wretched and poor do not warrant them) and open all locks of their own quality or lower. (2) AS A THIEF OF A GIVEN LEVEL -- randomly 6+1d8, i.e. level 7-14; OPEN LOCKS CHANCE IS 20% PLUS 5% PER THIEF LEVEL. (3) AS A MASTER KEY for one area, or more interestingly for every lock commissioned from one locksmith. (4) AS A MINOR MAGICAL ITEM, rating it as a high-level thief and/or granting major pick locks bonuses. A SKELETON KEY OPENS A LOCK BUT DOES NOT DISARM ANY TRAP attached to the lock or portal unless the original key would. Cannot be duplicated with a keymaking set. Cost is 'var.' in Table 31.

PHBR2 p.99. Heavy paper or, more usually, cloth soaked in tar, honey, treacle or anything suitably sticky. Slapped on a window before the pane is broken: the sticky surface holds the fragments together, CONSIDERABLY REDUCING NOISE both by cushioning the hammer blow and by stopping broken glass scattering across the floor beyond. IF SOMEONE IS WITHIN FAIRLY CLOSE LISTENING DISTANCE THE DM MAY MAKE A SECRET MOVE SILENTLY ROLL for the thief using this stratagem. Also used with a glass cutter, affixed to the centre of the pane so the cut disc can be pulled free.

PHBR2 p.100. A small block of wax, usually kept in a rigid container to keep it in one piece -- the equivalent of a large snuff-box. Used to take an impression of a key the thief wants duplicated later, when he has brief access to it and does not wish to risk borrowing it. From the impression a locksmith can cut a duplicate, or the thief can attempt one himself with a KEYMAKING SET -- at a PENALTY OF +2 to the Dexterity test, because the impression is a step removed from the key. With very soft wax, possibly heat-softened on the spot, a thief may take an impression of heavy seals, though an expert is needed for that kind of duplication or forgery. NOT THE SAME RECORD AS THE PHB'S SEALING/CANDLE WAX (1 gp per lb.), which is sold by weight for sealing and candles; both are kept.

PHBR2 p.99. A plant-derived flavouring. A small quantity dropped at a suitable place -- a stream bank the thief crosses, the base of a wall he traverses, a crossroads -- RUINS A TRACKING DOG'S SENSE OF SMELL UTTERLY FOR 1d4+1 HOURS if the dog reaches the spot. A SAVING THROW VS. POISON reduces this: the sense of smell is still ruined, but only for 1d4+1 TURNS. Neutralize poison or slow poison cast on the dog eliminates the effect, but the dog must still somehow pick the trail up further along. Effect on other trained tracking animals is up to the DM, though it should be detrimental to anything's sense of smell.

PHBR2 p.99. Four-pointed, always landing with one point more or less upright. THE BASE NUMBER IS 10 SCATTERED OVER 25 SQUARE FEET: anyone entering the area must make a SAVING THROW VS. PARALYZATION or step on one, taking damage and having movement reduced. HALF that number over the same area: save at +4. TWICE the number: save at an additional -2, to a -4 total. A CHARACTER MOVING AT ONE-THIRD NORMAL MOVEMENT NEED NOT SAVE. If the save is failed the pursuer can only move at ONE-THIRD normal rate for 2 HOURS, or until the damage is magically healed. Improvised caltrops are possible. PHBR2 bases its version on the tetsu-bishi entry in Oriental Adventures, which it considers superior to the Unearthed Arcana caltrops entry. A SEPARATE RECORD from the existing unattributed Caltrops (20); the two differ only in pack size.

PHBR2 p.99. A thick, foul-smelling liquid blended from various liquids obtained from diverse parts of cats together with a few secret ingredients. Very few people hold the recipe and those who do are well paid by thieves' guilds. Trained tracking dogs find it impossible to track when catstink is about, no matter how highly trained; a dog may smell it as far as half a mile downwind. Neutralize poison and similar spells do NOT help. Can also be used to delay a pursuer, who must make a saving throw vs. paralyzation before he can continue; this takes one round.

PHBR2 p.100. Dropped on the floor like aniseed to put a pursuing dog off the scent, but LESS EFFECTIVE: the dog gets a SAVING THROW VS. POISON to avoid the effect ABSOLUTELY, and on a failed save is unable to continue pursuit for 1d4+1 TURNS. MORE USEFULLY, scattered into the air: one packet fills a 10-FOOT CUBE and hangs there for 1d4 ROUNDS, and a DOG ENTERING THE AREA IN THAT TIME GETS NO SAVING THROW. Thrown right into a dog's face it likewise allows no save and the animal becomes HYSTERICAL AND TOTALLY UNCONTROLLABLE FOR AN HOUR.

PHBR2 p.100. A small metal pot about the size of a night-light candle with a hinged flip-up lid carrying a mirror on the inside -- often silver, which is why it is not cheap. The mirror directs the light and the lid doubles as a snuffer. Gives just enough light for the thief to work by, e.g. picking a lock in the dark, without giving him away: THE DIM FOCUSED LIGHT IS UNLIKELY TO BE VISIBLE BEYOND ABOUT 20 FEET, and is very dim even within that.

PHBR2 p.100. Boots with concealed compartments, commonly a swivelling heel: the heel is grasped and twisted firmly toward the inside surface, revealing a small hollow within. The compartments are very small -- typically one gem of moderate size, or up to four small ones. There is no externally visible built-up heel, but A THIEF WEARING THEM SUFFERS -5 TO ANY MOVE SILENTLY ROLL.

PHBR2 p.100. A general term for small spheres of glass, metal and the like. Loosed over a stone floor, they FORCE PURSUERS TO SLOW TO HALF NORMAL MOVEMENT RATE OR MAKE A DEXTERITY TEST; a failed test means the pursuer slips and spends a FULL ROUND getting up. Because marbles roll about a lot, a SMALL BAG OF 30 OR SO COVERS A 10' x 30' AREA or equivalent. Small stones and pebbles substitute only if polished and filed almost perfectly round -- a time-consuming business. A SEPARATE RECORD from the existing unattributed Marbles (100); the two differ only in pack size.

PHBR2 p.100. A general term for any highly abrasive powder irritating to the eyes -- powdered stone, pepper, dust soaked in onion juice, strong ammonium salts. Table 31 gives both cost and legality as 'var.' ONLY USEFUL THROWN RIGHT INTO THE EYES: this is a CALLED SHOT (DMG p.58) WITH AN ADDITIONAL DOUBLED PENALTY, FOR A TOTAL OF -8 ON THE ATTACK ROLL. The thrower's DEXTERITY BONUS APPLIES. The target's base AC IGNORES ANY ARMOR OR SHIELD except a helmet or helm; magical protection such as bracers of defense or a ring of protection does protect, as does Dexterity unless the attack has surprise. ON A HIT the effects are as the STINKING CLOUD spell except that they last 2d4+2 ROUNDS and NO SAVING THROW IS ALLOWED. Washing the eyes with plenty of water cuts the effect to one further round. No permanent damage to the eyes.

PHBR2 p.101. A ring with a flip-up lid, beneath which is a needle capable of delivering a dose of poison, knock-out drug or similar to a target. THE PRIMITIVE VERSION has the pin simply sitting in a small reservoir of liquid, so administration is haphazard: THE VICTIM RECEIVES A +2 BONUS TO ANY SAVING THROW against the effect. SUBTLER, MORE REFINED DESIGNS draw liquid up from a reservoir through the needle, so a NORMAL SAVING THROW applies, OR ONE AT -2. The DM decides which exist in the campaign; both may. A poison-delivery device, not a damage weapon -- the book gives it no damage.

PHBR2 p.101. As the iron pin ring -- a flip-lid ring concealing a needle for delivering poison or a knock-out drug -- in silver, which is the version that passes as jewellery. The book prices the two separately under one description. See the iron record for the saving-throw modifiers.

PHBR2 p.101. Strapped to the forearm to hold a dagger. VARIANTS ARE DROP SHEATHS, usually sewn into leather jackets or similar clothing, where release of the dagger is triggered mechanically (pressing a stud on the jacket sleeve) or by muscular stimuli against pressure pads (tensing the biceps firmly against the fist of the other arm). A SHEATH FOR a weapon, so it is equipment; record which of the character's weapons sits in it in the notes on the card, as with the PHBR1 secret-spring sheath.

PHBR2 p.102. A catchall title for specially modified boots with concealed blades. The blades must be small -- usually little bigger than a modern razor blade -- and are usually concealed in secret compartments in the heels (see Hollow Boots), though slender blades can be hidden in the soles. THE BOOK'S OWN VERDICT IS THAT THEY ARE OF LITTLE USE AS WEAPONS: their function is to slit pouches and purses, cut ropes and similar tasks, which is why this is an equipment record and not a weapon one.

PHBR2 p.102. A stout scabbard deliberately longer than the sword that fits it, leaving a length at the end which is a SEPARATE HOLLOW COMPARTMENT, usually reached by a sliding panel at the end. Used to conceal a great many things, smuggled either in (poisons, dog pepper, blinding powder) or out (gems and such). Some are so well-designed that the compartment can be entered from above or below, SO THE THIEF CAN USE THE FALSE SCABBARD AS A SNORKEL -- or more correctly an underwater breathing tube -- if he needs to stay concealed in water for any reason. Table 31 gives the weight as a range, 1-2.

PHBR2 p.102. A small oil-burning lamp with a reservoir of oil and a small wick sunk into an earthenware shell, used by CUPPING THE HANDS AROUND IT if cold would otherwise impair the thief's talents -- try picking a lock with frozen fingers in a cold clime. VIRTUALLY NO LIGHT IS PRODUCED; the aim is simply to warm the hands, which is why this is not a light source. The simplest version is a corked earthenware sphere filled with hot oil before the thief sets off, drawn from a pocket and held in the hands when needed.

PHBR2 p.102. Standard trappings for any self-respecting swindler. AD&D 2nd Edition has no gambling rules, so the book offers the DM two options. FIRST, IF THE GAMING PROFICIENCY IS USED: suitably marked cards or biased dice allow a -1 MODIFIER TO THE d20 CHECK (proficiencies work on low rolls). SECOND, IF THE GAME IS ACTUALLY PLAYED OUT and the Gaming proficiency is not used: the thief may REPLACE ANY ONE CARD DRAWN OR DIE THROWN if he has the suitable prop and MAKES A DEXTERITY TEST. Playing blackjack, drawn a king and a five, the effect is a REDRAW ON ONE CARD -- in all likelihood the five. WHEN ROLLING THE DEXTERITY TEST, IF THE d20 ROLL IS 18 OR MORE THE THIEF HAS BEEN SEEN CHEATING even if he makes the test successfully. FOR OBVIOUS REASONS THE DM SHOULD ROLL THIS TEST IN SECRET.

PHBR2 p.102. Loaded dice, the swindler's other standard prop. Same two options as marked cards: a -1 modifier to the d20 Gaming proficiency check, or -- if the game is played out without that proficiency -- the right to replace any one die thrown on a successful Dexterity test, with a natural 18+ meaning the thief was seen cheating anyway. The DM should roll that test in secret.
PHBR2 p.102. As the bone biased dice but in ivory, at four times the price -- the set a swindler works higher tables with. See the bone record for the cheating rules.

PHBR2 p.102. Large, wickerwork basketlike devices worn over the feet, coming to mid-calf height. The thief balances upright and propels himself across water with a paddle or oar. THE DM MAY INSIST ON A MOVE SILENTLY CHECK at some stage, and if anything happens to startle the thief -- an arrow whizzing past his head, a monster rising up in the water -- A DEXTERITY TEST MAY BE CALLED FOR TO AVOID FALLING IN. The book notes these belong most correctly in Kara-Tur, the land of Oriental Adventures and ninja, but could exist in any fantasy setting.
